title: 13 maps for the morning after the midterms
contentHtml:
At FiveThirtyEight, we sometimes experimented with showing readers a randomly selected cross-section of our election simulations to demonstrate how our models worked. I’m not sure that quite had the desired effect. Our customers tended to scroll through the simulations until they’d encounter one of the weirder maps, and then they’d sometimes use that as a way to express doubt about the forecast.

Paid subscribers get full access to our Election Night livestream and live blog with updates from our friends at The Argument, GD Politics and Slow Boring.

But weird things happen in elections. Barack Obama improbably1 won Indiana in 2008, and then the Hoosier State reverted back to basically where it had always been. On other occasions, results that seemed weird at the time made more sense in retrospect. Amidst a blue wave, Democratic Senator Bill Nelson lost in Florida in 2018, a state which at the time was only slightly to the right of the electoral tipping point. (Hillary Clinton had barely lost Florida in 2016.) That was the canary in the coal mine for a death spiral for Democrats in Florida.

Still, let’s give the “show me the maps!” concept one more spin. This time, we’ll curate things a bit more.2 From among the 40,000 simulations that FLIPR ran on Saturday, I’ve chosen 13 scenarios: nine or ten relatively normal cases, and then three or four deliberately weird ones.

To be fair, that distinction can get blurry. We’ll show you one map where Republicans hold the House as well as the Senate, something that’s rather unlikely if you believe FLIPR. In 2024, literally the exact most frequently-occurring map from our simulations “hit”, which involved Donald Trump winning precisely the seven canonical swing states that year but nothing beyond those. Often, however, maps are messier than people expect, especially in midterms.

But I’ll try to give you a representative flavor of the sorts of simulations FLIPR is cooking up. Not all of these are necessarily equally likely, however. They will include nine maps where Democrats flip the Senate and four where they don’t. That ratio is just slightly off from FLIPR’s roughly 3-to-1 odds for Democrats in the Senate, but close enough. There are lots of maps along the lines of “Democrats win 51 Senate seats, not including Texas” and “Democrats win 52 Senate seats, because James Talarico just gets barely over the finish line in Texas.”

Still, in curating these, I can’t get the Anna Karenina principle out of my head: “all happy families are alike [but] each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.” The maps where FLIPR kind of breaks — either there’s a Democratic mega-tsunami, or a polling bust — are more interesting than the ones where the model’s predictions are basically about right.

There’s also another point that I’ll try to layer in here. As much as we hope you’ll join us for our Election Night coverage, there’s a reasonably good chance that the midterm outcome, especially in the Senate, won’t be clear by Tuesday night or early Wednesday morning. One of the most important Senate races this year is in Alaska, which is slow to count its votes and also uses ranked-choice voting. All of this could get ugly, especially if Mary Peltola wins and Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy refuses to certify the vote. Maine is also a slow-counting state.

Even if everyone is on their best behavior, in about 20 percent of FLIPR simulations, control of the Senate will come down to exactly one state. If the United States “draws” one of those outcomes, and there are recounts, etc., it might take through next weekend or beyond to resolve who wins the Senate. The country has probably been lucky that during the Trump Era, most of the topline results have been relatively decisive: imagine how a replay of 2000 would play out now. (There’s no provision in FLIPR that accounts for irregularities in tallying the vote.) Perpetually tardy California doesn’t play a starring role this year in either the Senate or the House, at least.

But these are intended as “morning after” maps — in other words, what we’ll know as of, say, 8 a.m. on Wednesday. Based on some priors about how quickly each state counts its vote, I’ve applied different thresholds in different states toward when a preliminary result might be considered decisive. For instance, in a fast-counting state like North Carolina, I’ll assume that any result that eventually finishes outside 0.5 points, according to FLIPR, will de facto be known as of Wednesday morning, even if it hasn’t formally been “called” by the networks. In chronically slow-counting states like Alaska or California, I’ll raise that threshold to as high as a 3 percent margin. Thanks to FLIPR’s quasi-omniscience, I’ll show you who will eventually win in each simulation, but 1-2 Senate races, 1-2 gubernatorial races, and roughly a dozen House contests will likely remain ambiguous as of early Wednesday morning. These states and districts will be cross-hatched in yellow, indicating that they project to be close in the chosen simulation.

The base case

Just to get us started, let me first show you one of those relatively normal maps. For each simulation, I’ve calculated an “upset percentile”. After experimenting with more complicated algorithms3, this calculation is relatively simple. A race where a candidate who had a 49 percent chance of prevailing wins gets 1 Upset Point; a race where a candidate who had a 1 percent chance pulls a rabbit out of their hat is worth 49 Upset Points. These scores are then averaged out by branch, with the Senate getting 50 percent of the aggregate weight and the House and governorships getting 25 percent each. Then I translated that to a percentile ranking among all 40,000 simulations.4 Except for the first map and the last few, I’ve mostly chosen maps that have roughly average upset percentiles. When you’re forecasting 506 races, though, it would kind of be an upset if there are no major upsets. FLIPR is almost certain to get some races wrong.

Okay, this preamble has run on long enough. Here’s our first map, a deliberately conventional one. It’s FLIPR simulation #35949:

Believe them or not, this is pretty close to the base case given the polls. Yes, Democrats are ahead (slightly) in Kansas and Texas. So this map is only in the 5th percentile based on the number of upsets. It does have Democrats tending to win most of the close calls in the House. And David Jolly winning the Florida governorship in a mild upset, but Greg Abbott surviving by a fraction of a point in Texas following a recount. The Maine Senate race is close, but Democrats are doing well enough elsewhere that the overall disposition of the Senate is essentially certain by late Tuesday night either way.

Maps where it comes down to the wire

There are lots of other FLIPR simulations, though, where Democrats take the Senate by their chinny-chin-chin and the outcome looks more ambiguous on Election Night. Like this one, where the Maine, Michigan and Alaska Senate races are all uncalled on Tuesday night. Democrats eventually win the former two, but it could get messy. They also win the governorship in Georgia, but lose WI-Gov in an upset. This map reflects some D underperformance versus polls/forecasts in the Midwest — Republicans win Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska — but Democrats basically achieve “minimum viable product” by flipping North Carolina, Texas, Maine and Ohio, and just barely holding onto Michigan.
